title: Episode 90: Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition
itunes_title: Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition
description:
**Monday Immune Engager** — our weekly pick from the latest immune-engager digest.

**[Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44320-026-00246-1)**

*Molecular Systems Biology, 2026*

DOI: [10.1038/s44320-026-00246-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44320-026-00246-1)

**Question:** Do AI-designed minibinders function as CAR-T antigen-recognition domains, not just as high-affinity binders in isolation?

**Answer:** Across 12,000 designs from 28 teams, team hit rates ranged from 0.6% to 38.4% on an identical CD20 task. 707 designs showed significant enrichment, but of 10 validated individually only 4 showed CD20-specific lysis, all below the scFv control.

**Three takeaways**

1. Team hit rates spanned 0.6–38.4% on an identical task, though methods were self-selected, not assigned.
2. 98.9% of non-recovered designs used MPNN pipelines; a lysine-glutamate helix feature predicted dropout with 0.91 AUC.
3. Structure-confidence scores (pLDDT, ipTM) predicted nothing; a sequence-composition filter nearly doubled the functional hit rate.

source_metadata.title: Validation and analysis of 12,000 AI-driven CAR-T designs in the Bits to Binders competition
source_metadata.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Artificial intelligence (AI) methods for proteins have advanced rapidly, improving structure prediction and design, particularly for de novo binders. However, most evaluations emphasize binding affinity rather than higher-order biological function. We present
                    Bits to Binders
                    , a global competition evaluating de novo binder design in the context of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. Teams from 42 countries submitted 12,000 designs of 80-amino acid de novo minibinders targeting human CD20 as CAR binding domains. Designs were screened by pooled CAR-T proliferation, identifying 707 designs exhibiting significant CD20-specific enrichment, with team hit rates from 0.6% to 38.4%. Top-performing candidates were validated as individual constructs, measuring CD20-specific proliferation, expansion, cytokine production, and targeted cell lysis. We identified common design methodologies and factors correlated with DNA synthesis, expression, and target-specific T cell activation which nearly double the success rates when applied as a retrospective filter. We release this dataset as an open resource, with practical recommendations to support more effective AI-driven binder design.
